content: Discussion for the Year 4 part 1 roadmap. See #General announcements > Lean FRO
What does "Games" (in the first section) mean?

The "Trust" section seems to heavily focus on external checkers. Will this include coordination with new activity in #lean4lean that has followed the recent wave of soundness bugs? Is there any potential change in position of the FRO on the relevance of non-transitivity of definitional equality towards soundness, considering cases that like lean4#14807 where this seems like an essential component?

Isn't non-transitivity of defeq unavoidable? I mean

def b : Unit × Unit := (Unit.unit, Unit.unit)
theorem works (a c : Unit × Unit) : a = b ∧ b = c := ⟨rfl, rfl⟩  --works
theorem fails (a c : Unit × Unit) : a = c := rfl  --fails

is not gonna change any time soon, right?

In my understanding, the soundness bugs were implementation bugs, but once these are fixed there is no reason why non-transitivity of defeq would lead to soundness issues.

Michael Rothgang said:

Interactive web games?

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

In my understanding, the soundness bugs were implementation bugs, but once these are fixed there is no reason why non-transitivity of defeq would lead to soundness issues.

I don't want to comment at length when there are others more qualified to do so, but my reading of #lean4lean > Successes (especially the gist mwe posted there) makes me question the claim that these are purely "implementation bugs".
The fix in lean4#14807 definitely looks like implementation bug to me.

I perhaps should not have mentioned this specific case at all. I am not an expert in the type theory aspects here. The most important part of my question is whether there will be closer coordination between the official kernel and the verification efforts of lean4lean as part of this focus on external checkers.

On the standard library, the description of what's to come next is really generic.
Is it possible to expand on it ?
For example i know you guys are working on HTTP client and HTTPS. Is it set to be released for this Roadmap ?

As a user and library maintainer (LeanIO) built on top of the HTTP facilities i'm willing to help (feeback, code, review), just tell me if you want to.

Chris Henson said:

The most important part of my question is whether there will be closer coordination between the official kernel and the verification efforts of lean4lean as part of this focus on external checkers.

The lean4lean kernel will diverge from the official kernel however it needs/wants to, in order to get to a completely verified state as quickly as possible, after which we're intending to look at the divergences. But don't get hung up on these divergences. Diversity in kernels is a good thing. The priority should be getting lean4lean verified, and passing all the tests at the Lean Kernel Arena, rather than worrying about exact alignment with the default kernel. I'm looking forward to turning lean4lean on in https://lean-lang.org/eval/, and hopefully Mathlib too, once it is ready.

If you're interested in this, review of my open PR lean4lean#32 would be great. It is a giant AI-written diff, so even just suggestions about how to decompose it, or any opinions about its sanity, would be great. There's an even larger branch, still WIP, at https://github.com/kim-em/lean4lean/tree/agent/verify-inductives.

Alfredo Moreira-Rosa said:

For example i know you guys are working on HTTP client and HTTPS. Is it set to be released for this Roadmap ?

@Alfredo Moreira-Rosa this is all being actively worked on and reviewed, by Sophia and Julia:

  • feat: add HTTP client foundation and configuration lean4#14546 (+435/−5)
  • feat: add HTTP client connection lean4#14547 (+2782/−65)
  • feat: add HTTP client lean4#14548 (+3793/−3, redirect handling, transport-agnostic)
  • feat: introduce Std.Internal.SSL.Context lean4#14064 (+2049/−8)
  • feat: introduce Std.Internal.SSL.Session lean4#14065 (+3242/−81) (in-memory TLS state machine over OpenSSL BIOs, client and server sides)
  • feat: introduce Std.Async.TCP.SSL lean4#14066 (+2517/−4) (the TLS-capable socket)
Are there plans to work on a better verion of plausible, one where things are at expression level and where counterexamples are generated, not just messages? A design was suggested by @Eric Wieser .
My guess is that this has lost a lot of its value, since now impossible + LLMs are reasonable counterexample generators.
(I'm not arguing that LLMs are a replacement for good tactics, but plausible is unlike most other tactics in that it only exists transitively during development)
Thanks @Eric Wieser . I did not know about impossible. I will start using that where I intended to use plausible.
Does impossible accept a list of tactics to try (or should/could it be combined with try)?

I don’t think plausible has lost its value, systematic counter example generation is still a very useful and poweful tool, and I hope that eventually™ we can make it better and part of the default experience.

The impossible tactic is a building block for try to report impossibilities, it doesn't do any search of its own.

@Joachim Breitner I take it that eventually means nobody is working on it now.

Unfortunately I am also in the middle of too many things. If and when I get time to work on it (or rather a counterexample finder, which may not end up as the official plausible), I will check the statue.

Are there any plans to improve semantic syntax highlighting?
It’s literally the face of the language — something that every Lean user has in front of them 100% of the time while working with Lean
It seems like relatively small investments in this area could significantly improve the overall UX :thinking:

Evgeniy Kuznetsov said:

something that every Lean user has in front of them 100% of the time while working with Lean

(not entirely true anymore... some Lean projects I now jump from markdown spec to reviewing the rendered Verso manual pages! :-)

But did you have concrete suggestions / issues to point at?

I would like to add something about grind extensions - while it seems to be more and more widely used by LLMs and seems successful in many domains, it is very unfriendly for human proof reviewers since all they see is that the technique managed to prove the statement and at best might extract a giant proof term from it. This may also have performance implications considering the grind's overall search should rerun on each check. I still think it would be great idea if the grind could be translated to something more transparent and less performance heavy via grind? similarly to aesop? whenever possible. Not sure how feasible this seems to everyone else but just wanted to illustrate to usability pain points some of us have with it.
